sources.title: Sarojini Naidu (Q250165), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Sarojini Naidu', description 'Indian poet, politician, governor of the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh from 1947 to 1949', Korean label 사로지니 나이두, instance of human, born 13 February 1879, died 2 March 1949. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Kenneth R. Shepherd, 'Naidu, Sarojini (1879-1949)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full, with its bibliography). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: poet in English (The Golden Threshold, 1905; The Bird of Time, 1912; The Broken Wing, 1917) and nationalist leader; advised by the critic Edmund Gosse to set her poems in India, a speaker for women's education and Hindu-Muslim unity, associate of Gandhi, returned a government medal over the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, president of the Indian National Congress in 1925 (succeeding Gandhi), jailed in 1930-31, 1932-33 and 1942-43, first governor of the United Provinces (Uttar Pradesh) from 1947. Drawn largely from the biographies by Padmini Sengupta and Tara Ali Baig and from Makarand Paranjape and K. R. Ramachandran Nair, so admiring in tone.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sarojini Naidu' (read in full): her argument that the nationalist cause could not be separated from women's liberation; the 1917 delegation with Annie Besant and Herabai Tata to the Secretary of State for India and the Viceroy on women's votes; her 1924 travel to East and South Africa for Indians there; her 1925 election as the first Indian woman president of the Congress; North American lecture tour 1928-29; prison sentences in 1930, 1932 and 1942-43; the 1931 Round Table Conference; governor of the United Provinces from 1947 and member of the constituent assembly; election as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 1914. Short reference article.

'Sarojini Naidu', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). Reference biography with critical comment: quotes Gosse's judgement that her early poems were skilful but Western in feeling and his advice to set them among India's mountains, gardens and temples; says her verse is lyrical and musical but tends to become monotonous, that her claim to lasting fame rests more on her career as a nationalist leader, and that her poetry was 'transmuted into oratory'; names her as a founder of the Women's India Association with Annie Besant and Margaret Cousins, Gandhi's envoy to South Africa and a mediator with the Muslim League. States she was imprisoned five times, which conflicts with the three terms in other sources.

Abdulla K. Badsha, 'Sarojini Naidu', EBSCO Research Starters (History), 2024 (read in full, with bibliography): her poetry's blend of Eastern themes and Western forms and her apology that she sang 'just as birds do'; negotiation roles in Britain (the 1919 Home Rule League delegation and the 1931 Round Table Conference); three prison terms; travel to Africa and the United States to win support; organising women's groups for education; friendship with Jinnah while remaining in the Congress; as governor she restrained the majority on language questions. Reference article for students, admiring.

Webb Miller (United Press), 'Natives beaten down by police in India salt bed raid', dispatch from Dharasana, 21 May 1930, UPI Archives (read in full; the dispatch was delayed by censorship). EYEWITNESS REPORT: describes the poetess-leader Mrs Sarojini Naidu opening the raid of 2,500 volunteers on the Dharasana Salt Works with an impassioned speech ('Although Gandhi's body is in prison, his soul goes with you'), the volunteers' refusal to resist police clubs, 260 injured by the reporter's count, her directing operations near the front and her arrest by a British official. Contemporary independent reporting by a foreign correspondent.

Nazma Yeasmeen Haque, 'The world of Sarojini Naidu', The Daily Star (Dhaka), 10 January 2014 (read in full; literary feature drawing on Sengupta and other biographies): Pattabhi Sitaramayya's remark that her 1925 presidential address was perhaps the shortest and sweetest ever delivered at the Congress, a New York Times description of her rise to the presidency, the 1928-29 North American tour reported in Young India, her habit of attending Urdu and Hindi poetry gatherings, and her first weeks as governor. Appreciative feature, not scholarship.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_naidu_upi, src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ewb, src_naidu_dailystar | 1925-1947 | eyewitness news dispatch, reference biography, reference biography, appreciative feature] A foreign correspondent's 1930 dispatch records that at Dharasana her speech launched 2,500 volunteers on the salt-works raid; the reference entries say her speaking in English was her greatest contribution, that she swayed audiences in India and abroad (the 1928-29 North American tour, a mission to South Africa), and the Congress historian Sitaramayya is quoted on her 1925 address. Most of the praise is admiring biographers quoted in the Gale entries, and the eyewitness record covers one speech. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.64 to 74 / 0.58 because the independent evidence is a single event and the rest is admiring secondary praise.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_naidu_upi, src_naidu_britannica, src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ebsco | 1919-1943 | eyewitness news dispatch, reference article, reference biography, reference article] The eyewitness records her directing the Dharasana action from near the front while police charged with clubs, and her arrest there; three reference sources list jail terms in 1930, 1932 and 1942-43 (a fourth says five, so the count is uncertain), and the Women in World History entry says she returned a government medal over the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The confrontations were non-violent civil disobedience, which limits reading them as physical risk-taking. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.54 because the eyewitness covers one event and the sources disagree on the number of imprisonments.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_naidu_britannica, src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ewb, src_naidu_upi | 1917-1949 | reference article, reference biography, reference biography, eyewitness news dispatch] She co-led the 1917 women's-suffrage delegation, helped found the Women's India Association, was elected Congress president in 1925, was called the poetess-leader at Dharasana by a correspondent who watched her direct the raid, and held the governorship from 1947. The presidency and governorship were elective or appointed posts, and the same list recurs in each reference entry. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 68 / 0.52 because only the Dharasana report is independent of the shared biographical sources.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_naidu_britannica, src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ebsco, src_naidu_ewb | 1915-1949 | reference article, reference biography, reference article, reference biography] Across three decades she worked on four public causes named in the entries (national freedom, women's emancipation and education, youth, and Hindu-Muslim unity): she argued that the nationalist cause could not be separated from women's liberation, joined the 1917 suffrage delegation, organised women's groups for education, and acted as envoy and mediator. The entries rely on the same Sengupta and Baig biographies, so the pattern is well attested but not independently corroborated. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.58 to 70 / 0.54 for that shared source base.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_naidu_ewb, src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ebsco, src_naidu_britannica, src_naidu_dailystar | 1905-1949 | reference biography, reference biography, reference article, reference article, appreciative feature] She published three volumes of verse in 1905, 1912 and 1917 that the entries describe as built on varied metre, rhyme and imagery drawn from Indian life, was elected a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 1914, kept a literary salon in Bombay, and attended Urdu and Hindi poetry gatherings. The score reflects her documented cultivation of the craft, not the quality of the poetry, which one entry judges monotonous.

adaptability.rationale: [src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ewb, src_naidu_ebsco | 1898-1947 | reference biography, reference biography, reference article] Two documented shifts: after Gosse's advice she moved the setting of her poems from English models to Indian scenes (three entries), and after 1917 she wrote little substantial poetry and became a full-time public speaker and organiser, later an envoy abroad and a provincial governor. The shifts are well attested but all come from the same biographical family. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.48 to 64 / 0.46.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_naidu_britannica, src_naidu_wwh, src_naidu_ebsco | 1905-1949 | reference article, reference biography, reference article] Documented output in English-language poetry, mass oratory, women's organisations, delegations and lecture tours abroad, and later a governorship. The work stays within literature and public life and the sources do not treat range as a trait. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.48 to 62 / 0.46 because the three entries share one source base.
